summary: This 2015 Scientific Reports study describes a rhesus monkey model of alcohol-induced liver disease that mirrors human alcoholic liver disease (ALD) progression. Sixteen monkeys were fed an increasing ethanol solution for about 3 years, with three controls, and were assessed by ultrasound, liver histology, serum chemistry and hepatic gene expression arrays. The authors report steatosis and fibrosis along with gene expression changes resembling those seen in human fatty liver and liver cancer, and argue the model could aid ALD drug development.
one_line: A 2015 study describing a rhesus monkey model of alcohol-induced liver steatosis and fibrosis that reflects human ALD progression and hepatic gene expression.
key_facts: The study was published online on 7 October 2015 in Scientific Reports (Sci Rep. 2015; 5: 15019) with PMID 26442469.
Sixteen rhesus monkeys were fed an alcohol solution for 3 years, with three control animals maintained on the same diet without alcohol.
The mean daily alcohol intake over the 3-year period was 9.6 g/kg per day (range 6.2–12.1 g/kg per day), or 24% of total daily caloric intake.
The ethanol concentration started at 5% (v/v) and was increased by 5% each week until it reached a final concentration of 25%.
Alcohol-fed monkeys showed steatosis, inflammation and ballooning degeneration, with fibrosis confirmed by Masson staining.
Alcohol-fed monkeys with liver fibrosis had significantly increased plasma GGT, and serum HA and LN were elevated compared to controls (P < 0.05).
Genes CPT1A, FASN, LEPR, RXRA, IGFBP1, PPARGC1A and SLC2A4 were elevated 3- to 6-fold in monkeys with liver steatosis.
Genes CYP7A1, HMGCR, GCK and PNPLA3 were down-regulated 3- to 23-fold in monkeys with liver steatosis.
Genes E2F1, OPCML, FZD7, IGFBP1 and LEF1 were elevated 3- to 9-fold in monkeys with liver fibrosis.
Previous rhesus studies using a 7% ethanol solution took 3–5 years to induce steatosis and fibrosis at 4.6 g/kg per day, while this study shortened the duration to under 3 years.
The study states that the monkeys were 9 to 12 years old and were supplied by Kunming Biomed International.
Histology grading defined mild, moderate and severe fat scores as 10–15%, 15–30% and more than 40% vacuolated hepatocytes, respectively.
The authors state that the AST/ALT ratio is greater than 1.5 in humans when liver injury is considered to be ALD.
The authors state that the study provides the first demonstration that alcohol induces changes in hepatic gene expression of markers related to fatty liver and liver cancer in rhesus models.
